  • In metaphase I, homologous chromosomes arrange themselves in pairs at the equator.
  • In anaphase II, centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles.
  • Prophase I differs from prophase II: in prophase I homologous chromosomes form pairs and crossing over takes place; in prophase II no crossing over takes place and chromosomes are single.
  • When homologous chromosomes fail to separate, it is called non-disjunction.

mcqs.q: In organisms, meiosis produces .........
mcqs.why: Meiosis produces gametes in organisms. It does not produce new somatic (body) cells; somatic cells are made by mitosis.

mcqs.q: A spore mother cell produces spores by .........
mcqs.why: Spores are produced by meiosis: the spore mother cell divides by meiosis to form spores with half the chromosome number.

mcqs.q: Meiosis I is called reduction division because .........
options: in it the number of chromosomes becomes half
mcqs.why: Meiosis I is the reduction division because during it the number of chromosomes becomes half, which is why the resulting cells are haploid.

mcqs.q: How does the chromosome number stay constant generation after generation?
options: In meiosis the number becomes half and in fertilisation it becomes full again
The number never changes in any division
mcqs.why: The number stays constant because meiosis halves it in gametes and fertilisation restores the full number when the gametes fuse.

mcqs.q: Pachytene is a stage of prophase I in which .........
options: chromosomes thicken and crossing over takes place
mcqs.why: In pachytene the chromosomes thicken and crossing over takes place between homologous chromosomes. It is one of the sub-stages of prophase I.

mcqs.q: A bivalent is .........
options: a pair of homologous chromosomes formed in meiosis
mcqs.why: A bivalent is a pair of homologous chromosomes formed in meiosis when the homologues come together during prophase I.

mcqs.q: Diakinesis is .........
options: the first stage of prophase II
the stage in which DNA is copied
the last stage of prophase I, in which chromosomes thicken further and the nuclear membrane disappears
mcqs.why: Diakinesis is the last stage of prophase I: the chromosomes thicken further and the nuclear membrane disappears, ending prophase I.

mcqs.q: In anaphase II of meiosis .........
options: centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate
mcqs.why: In anaphase II the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles, as in mitosis.

mcqs.q: The process in which homologous chromosomes fail to separate is called .........
mcqs.why: When homologous chromosomes do not separate, it is called non-disjunction. Crossing over, by contrast, is the normal exchange that happens at chiasmata.

mcqs.q: At the end of meiosis .........
options: two cells with full chromosome number form
four gametes form with half the number of chromosomes
mcqs.why: Meiosis ends with four gametes, each having half the number of chromosomes, because the cell passes through two divisions after one DNA copying.

lessons.title: Definition of Enzymes
lessons.notes_html:
Metabolism

The chemical reactions taking place in living organisms are together called metabolic reactions. Metabolism includes both kinds of reactions.

TypeMeaning
Anabolism (constructive reactions)Large molecules are formed from small molecules, and energy is spent.
Catabolism (destructive reactions)Large molecules break down into small molecules, and energy is released.

Metabolic processes are of two types: anabolism and catabolism.

Conditions Needed for Chemical Reactions

Chemical reactions need specific conditions so that they can proceed correctly. Those conditions are:

  • Temperature
  • pH

Activation Energy

Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction.

Enzymes lower the activation energy of a chemical reaction. Enzymes bind with the substrate and lower the energy needed to start the reaction, so the reaction happens quickly.

Definition of Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in the cell.

Most enzymes are made of proteins, so enzymes are proteins in nature.

mcqs.q: Metabolic reactions are:
mcqs.why: Metabolism includes both constructive reactions, called anabolism, and destructive reactions, called catabolism, so metabolic reactions are of both kinds.

mcqs.q: Metabolic processes are of ......... types.
mcqs.why: Metabolism has two types: constructive reactions (anabolism) and destructive reactions (catabolism). It is not one, three or four types.

mcqs.q: In anabolic reactions, ......... molecules are formed.
mcqs.why: In anabolic reactions large molecules are formed from small molecules. Small molecules are the starting material, not the product formed.

mcqs.q: What is anabolism?
options: The breaking down of large molecules
The minimum energy needed to start a reaction
The process in which large molecules are formed from small molecules
mcqs.why: Anabolism is the process in which large molecules are formed from small molecules. Breaking down large molecules is catabolism, the opposite process.

mcqs.q: What is catabolism?
options: The forming of large molecules from small ones
The part of an enzyme where the substrate binds
The process in which large molecules break down into small molecules
A substance that increases enzyme action
mcqs.why: Catabolism is the process in which large molecules break down into small molecules. Forming large molecules from small ones is anabolism instead.

mcqs.q: What is activation energy?
options: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction
The energy released at the end of a reaction
The total energy of a cell
The energy stored in an enzyme
mcqs.why: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction. Enzymes work by lowering this energy so the reaction can begin more easily.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between anabolism and catabolism?
options: There is no difference between them
Anabolism breaks molecules and catabolism builds them
Anabolism releases energy and catabolism spends energy
In anabolism large molecules are formed from small molecules and energy is spent, while in catabolism large molecules break down into small ones and energy is released
mcqs.why: In anabolism large molecules are formed from small molecules and energy is spent. In catabolism large molecules break down into small ones and energy is released.

mcqs.q: Chemical reactions need specific conditions so that they can proceed correctly. What are those conditions?
mcqs.why: Chemical reactions need the correct temperature and pH to proceed correctly. Light and colour are not the conditions named for these reactions.

mcqs.q: Enzymes ......... the activation energy of a chemical reaction.
mcqs.why: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction. They bind with the substrate and lower the energy needed to start the reaction, so it happens quickly.

mcqs.q: Enzymes are best defined as:
options: Biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in the cell
The end products of chemical reactions
mcqs.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in the cell. The substance an enzyme acts on is called the substrate, not the enzyme.

lessons.title: Characteristics of Enzymes
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in the cell. Their properties are:

  • Mostly made of proteins.
  • Act on a specific substrate.
  • Are not changed at the end of the reaction.
  • A small amount is enough.
  • Are sensitive to temperature and pH.
  • Have no effect on the equilibrium of a reaction; they only speed up its rate.

The presence of enzymes also does not affect the amount of the end product; it only speeds up the rate of the reaction.

Important Terms

TermMeaning
SubstrateThe substance on which an enzyme acts.
Active siteThe small part of the enzyme where the substrate binds.
CofactorThe non-protein part of an enzyme which is necessary for the action of the enzyme.
Prosthetic groupA cofactor which is firmly attached to the enzyme.
HoloenzymeA complete enzyme formed by the combination of apoenzyme and cofactor.

Activators and Inhibitors

ActivatorInhibitor
Activators are substances that increase the action of enzymes.Inhibitors are substances that stop or reduce the action of enzymes.

Acting with inhibitors is not a property of enzymes; inhibitors reduce their action.

Factors Affecting the Action of Enzymes

FactorEffect
TemperatureAction is best at a suitable temperature. As the temperature rises, the initial reaction rate increases, until the enzyme is damaged at very high temperature.
pHEvery enzyme has a suitable pH. The pH at which an enzyme works best is called its optimum pH. Extreme change in pH can cause denaturation of enzymes.
Amount of substrateAs the amount of substrate increases, the action of the enzyme speeds up, until all the enzymes are busy; after that the rate does not increase further.
Activators and inhibitorsActivators increase the action, and inhibitors reduce it.

pH, amount of substrate and temperature affect the action of enzymes; organic gradients do not.

Use of Enzymes in Factories

In factories, enzymes are used in making:

  • Paper
  • Bread
  • Beverages
  • Washing products

mcqs.q: Enzymes are:
mcqs.why: Most enzymes are made of proteins, so enzymes are proteins in nature. They are biological catalysts, not carbohydrates, lipids or minerals.

mcqs.q: All of the following are properties of enzymes except one. Which is the one?
options: Enzymes are sensitive to pH change
The action of enzymes takes place with inhibitors
mcqs.why: Enzymes speed up reactions, are sensitive to pH change and have an active site. Inhibitors reduce the action of enzymes, so acting with inhibitors is not a property of enzymes.

mcqs.q: What is the pH at which enzymes work best called?
mcqs.why: Every enzyme has an optimum pH at which its work is best. A pH far from this value does not give the best action and extreme change can denature the enzyme.

mcqs.q: Enzyme action can be increased by .........
mcqs.why: Activators are substances that increase the action of enzymes. Inhibitors do the opposite: they stop or reduce the action of enzymes.

mcqs.q: The small part of the enzyme where the substrate binds is called .........
mcqs.why: The substrate binds at the active site of the enzyme. A cofactor is the non-protein part of an enzyme, and a holoenzyme is the complete enzyme.

mcqs.q: What happens to the rate of reaction when the temperature rises?
options: It increases, until the enzyme is damaged
mcqs.why: When the temperature rises, the rate of reaction increases, until the enzyme is damaged. At very high temperature the enzyme can no longer work properly.

mcqs.q: Extreme change in pH can cause ......... of enzymes.
mcqs.why: Extreme change in pH can cause denaturation of enzymes. Enzymes are sensitive to pH and work best only at their optimum pH.

mcqs.q: What is a cofactor?
options: The non-protein part of an enzyme which is necessary for the action of the enzyme
The substance on which an enzyme acts
A substance that stops enzyme action
mcqs.why: A cofactor is the non-protein part of an enzyme which is necessary for the action of the enzyme. The substance an enzyme acts on is the substrate.

mcqs.q: How are enzymes used in factories?
options: In making paper, bread, beverages and washing products
They are not used in factories
mcqs.why: In factories enzymes are used in making paper, bread, beverages and washing products. These are the uses given for enzymes in industry.

mcqs.q: How does substrate concentration affect enzyme action?
options: More substrate always slows the enzyme down
As the amount of substrate increases, the action speeds up until all the enzymes are busy; after that the rate does not increase further
Substrate amount has no effect at all
The rate increases without any limit
mcqs.why: As the amount of substrate increases, the action of the enzyme speeds up, until all the enzymes are busy; after that the rate does not increase further.

lessons.title: Mechanism of Enzyme Action
lessons.notes_html:
How an Enzyme Works

A substrate is the substance on which an enzyme acts. The active site is the part of the enzyme where the substrate binds.

  • The substrate binds at the active site of the enzyme.
  • Enzymes bind with the substrate and lower the energy needed to start the reaction.
  • Because the activation energy is lowered, the reaction happens quickly.
  • The presence of enzymes does not affect the amount of the end product; it only speeds up the rate of the reaction.
  • The enzyme itself is not changed at the end of the reaction.

Two Models of Enzyme Action

ModelMain idea
Lock and key modelEnzyme and substrate have specially matching geometric shapes, so they fit each other like a lock and a key.
Induced fit modelThe active site continuously changes its shape until the substrate binds to it; the active site changes its shape according to the substrate.

In short: in the lock and key model the shapes already match, while in the induced fit model the active site changes its shape to fit the substrate.

mcqs.q: The active site continuously changes its shape until the substrate binds to it. Which model does this statement describe?
mcqs.why: In the induced fit model the active site changes its shape according to the substrate until the substrate binds to it. The lock and key model has already matching shapes.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct statement about the lock and key model.
options: The active site keeps changing its shape
Enzyme and substrate have specially matching geometric shapes
The enzyme is changed at the end of the reaction
The substrate binds anywhere on the enzyme
mcqs.why: In the lock and key model, enzyme and substrate fit each other like a lock and a key because they have specially matching geometric shapes.

mcqs.q: How do enzymes lower the activation energy?
options: By raising the temperature of the cell
By changing the end product of the reaction
By binding with the substrate and lowering the energy needed to start the reaction, so the reaction happens quickly
By stopping the substrate from reacting
mcqs.why: Enzymes bind with the substrate and lower the energy needed to start the reaction, so the reaction happens quickly. They do not change the end product.

mcqs.q: How does the presence of enzymes affect the end product of a reaction?
options: It increases the amount of the end product
It decreases the amount of the end product
It changes the end product into a different substance
It does not affect the amount of the end product; it only speeds up the rate of the reaction, and the enzyme itself is not changed
mcqs.why: The presence of enzymes does not affect the amount of the end product. It only speeds up the rate of the reaction, and the enzyme itself is not changed at the end.

mcqs.q: What is a substrate?
options: The substance on which an enzyme acts
The small part of an enzyme where binding takes place
A substance that stops enzyme action
The end product of every reaction
mcqs.why: A substrate is the substance on which an enzyme acts. The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds is called the active site, not the substrate.

mcqs.q: What is the active site?
options: The non-protein part of an enzyme
The part of the enzyme where the substrate binds
A cofactor firmly attached to the enzyme
The complete enzyme made of apoenzyme and cofactor
mcqs.why: The active site is the part of the enzyme where the substrate binds. A complete enzyme formed from apoenzyme and cofactor is a holoenzyme.

mcqs.q: Enzymes ......... the activation energy of a chemical reaction.
mcqs.why: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction. Lowering this minimum energy needed to start the reaction makes the reaction happen quickly.

mcqs.q: What happens to the enzyme itself at the end of the reaction?
options: It is changed into the substrate
It becomes part of the end product
mcqs.why: The enzyme itself is not changed at the end of the reaction. It only speeds up the rate of the reaction without affecting the amount of end product.

mcqs.q: Where does the substrate bind on the enzyme?
options: It does not bind to the enzyme at all
mcqs.why: The substrate binds at the active site of the enzyme. The active site is the small part of the enzyme made for this binding.

mcqs.q: Why does a reaction happen quickly in the presence of an enzyme?
options: Because the enzyme raises the pH of the cell
Because the enzyme lowers the energy needed to start the reaction
Because the enzyme increases the amount of end product
Because the enzyme changes the equilibrium of the reaction
mcqs.why: The reaction happens quickly because the enzyme binds with the substrate and lowers the energy needed to start it. Enzymes have no effect on the equilibrium of a reaction.

lessons.title: Specificity of Enzymes
lessons.notes_html:
Why Enzymes Are Specific

Enzymes are specific in nature because the active site of each enzyme fits only one particular substrate.

One property of enzymes is that they act on a specific substrate. Because the active site fits only that substrate, one enzyme does not act on other substances in the same way.

Examples of Specific Action

EnzymeSubstrate it acts on
LipaseLipids
TrypsinProtein

Protein does not act on carbohydrate. That is why, in the pairing Protein to carbohydrate, this pair is the odd one out: lipase acts on lipids and trypsin acts on protein, but protein does not act on carbohydrate.

Many Enzymes in the Human Body

In the human body there are more than 1000 enzymes. Each one acts on its own specific substrate, which is possible because the active site of each enzyme fits only one particular substrate.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific in nature?
options: Because every enzyme works at every pH
Because enzymes are changed at the end of a reaction
Because the active site of each enzyme fits only one particular substrate
Because a large amount of every enzyme is needed
mcqs.why: Enzymes are specific in nature because the active site of each enzyme fits only one particular substrate. An enzyme therefore acts on that substrate and not on others.

mcqs.q: Choose the odd one out.
options: An enzyme acting on its specific substrate
mcqs.why: Protein does not act on carbohydrate, so that pair is the odd one out. Lipase acts on lipids and trypsin acts on protein, which are correct specific actions.

mcqs.q: In the human body there are more than ......... enzymes.
mcqs.why: In the human body there are more than 1000 enzymes. Each of these enzymes acts on its own specific substrate through its active site.

mcqs.q: Lipase acts on:
mcqs.why: Lipase acts on lipids. This is an example of the specific nature of enzymes: each enzyme acts on its own particular substrate.

mcqs.q: Trypsin acts on:
options: The active site of another enzyme
mcqs.why: Trypsin acts on protein. Lipase, by contrast, acts on lipids, and protein does not act on carbohydrate.

mcqs.q: One enzyme normally acts on:
options: Only one particular substrate, because its active site fits only that substrate
All lipids and all proteins together
mcqs.why: An enzyme acts on a specific substrate because its active site fits only one particular substrate. That fitting is the reason for the specific nature of enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which of the following does NOT take place?
options: A substrate binds at the active site
mcqs.why: Protein does not act on carbohydrate, so that action does not take place. Lipase acting on lipids and trypsin acting on protein are the correct specific actions.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches an enzyme with its substrate?
mcqs.why: Lipase acts on lipids, so that is the correctly matched pair. Trypsin acts on protein, not lipids, and protein does not act on carbohydrate.

mcqs.q: Which statement is one of the properties of enzymes?
options: Enzymes act on any substrate at all
Enzymes are changed at the end of the reaction
Enzymes act on a specific substrate
mcqs.why: Acting on a specific substrate is a property of enzymes. Enzymes have an active site and are not changed at the end of the reaction.

mcqs.q: The active site is important for the specificity of an enzyme because:
options: It fits only one particular substrate
It changes the amount of the end product
mcqs.why: The active site of each enzyme fits only one particular substrate, and that is why enzymes are specific in nature. It does not fit every substrate.

lessons.title: 7.1 Bioenergetics and the Role of ATP
lessons.notes_html:
What is Bioenergetics?

Bioenergetics is the science in which the conversion and use of energy in organisms is studied. The conversion of free energy into different forms in organisms is also called bioenergetics.

Energy and Its Source

Energy is the ability to do work. The source of energy is only the sun — the sun is the original source of energy.

Plants use light energy to make use of simple inorganic molecules, water and carbon dioxide. In this way, energy from the sun enters living organisms through plants.

Food Chain

A food chain is the line of organisms in which one organism eats another and energy moves forward. Energy therefore passes from one organism to the next along the food chain.

Oxidation

Oxidation is the reaction in which electrons and protons are lost. The loss of electrons and protons is called an oxidation reaction.

ATP — The Treasure of Cellular Energy

The treasure of cellular energy is ATP. Energy in organisms is stored in a special molecule called ATP, and the energy obtained by breaking down a food molecule is stored in the form of ATP.

PointDetail
Energy stored inATP — a special molecule in organisms
Energy in each mole of ATP7.3 Kcal/mole
Original source of energyThe sun
Energy from breaking down foodStored in the form of ATP

How Chemical Energy is Transferred

Chemical energy is stored in food molecules. In respiration, that energy is transferred into ATP, and then it is used in the activities of the cell.

  • Chemical energy is stored in food molecules.
  • In respiration, this energy is transferred into ATP.
  • The ATP is then used for the activities of the cell.

mcqs.q: What is bioenergetics?
options: The science of the structure of bones
The science in which the conversion and use of energy in organisms is studied
The science of blood circulation only
The science of making food in plants only
mcqs.why: Bioenergetics is the science in which the conversion and use of energy in organisms is studied. It is about how free energy is converted into different forms in organisms, not about bones or circulation.

mcqs.q: What is energy?
mcqs.why: Energy is defined in the source as the ability to do work. Organisms need energy for all their activities, and that energy is stored and transferred in the form of ATP.

mcqs.q: What is the only source of energy?
mcqs.why: The source answers clearly that the original source of energy is only the sun. Plants use the sun's light energy to use water and carbon dioxide, and energy then moves forward through the food chain.

mcqs.q: What is the loss of electrons and protons called?
mcqs.why: The loss of electrons and protons is called oxidation, and oxidation is the reaction in which electrons and protons are lost. Fermentation and photolysis are different processes described elsewhere in this unit.

mcqs.q: In which special molecule is energy stored in organisms?
mcqs.why: Energy in organisms is stored in a special molecule called ATP. ATP is also called the treasure of cellular energy, because food energy is transferred into ATP and then used in cell activities.

mcqs.q: How much energy does each mole of ATP store?
mcqs.why: Each mole of ATP stores 7.3 Kcal of energy. This is the figure given in the source for one mole of ATP, while 2827 kJ is the energy from one mole of glucose, not from ATP.

mcqs.q: What is a food chain?
options: A line of leaves on a plant
A cycle of water in nature
The line of organisms in which one organism eats another and energy moves forward
mcqs.why: A food chain is the line of organisms in which one organism eats another and energy moves forward. This is how energy that first enters plants passes on to other organisms.

mcqs.q: What do plants use to make use of simple inorganic molecules, water and carbon dioxide?
mcqs.why: Plants use light energy to make use of simple inorganic molecules, water and carbon dioxide. This light energy comes from the sun, which is the original source of energy for organisms.

mcqs.q: In what form is the energy obtained by breaking down a food molecule stored?
mcqs.why: The energy obtained by breaking down a food molecule is stored in the form of ATP. For this reason ATP is called the treasure of cellular energy, ready to be used in the activities of the cell.

mcqs.q: What is the treasure of cellular energy, and how is chemical energy transferred?
options: Starch; it is used directly without change
ATP; chemical energy stored in food is transferred into ATP in respiration and then used in cell activities
Glucose; it is never changed into any other form
Oxygen; it carries food energy to the food chain
mcqs.why: The treasure of cellular energy is ATP. Chemical energy is stored in food molecules; in respiration that energy is transferred into ATP, and then it is used in the activities of the cell.

lessons.title: 7.2 Photosynthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Photosynthesis — The Basic Molecule Formed

In photosynthesis, glucose is basically formed. Plants use light energy to make use of simple inorganic molecules, water and carbon dioxide, and glucose is the basic molecule formed during this process.

  • Basic molecule formed: glucose
  • Photosynthesis is the only process that produces free oxygen.
  • In plants, glucose is converted into starch, cellulose, sucrose and other substances.

The Chloroplast

The chloroplast is a double-membrane organelle. Different pigments in the chloroplast absorb different light.

PartDetail
StromaThe semi-fluid protein liquid of the chloroplast, in which grana float
GranaStacks of thylakoids in the chloroplast
ThylakoidThe place where the light-dependent (light) reaction takes place
PigmentsDifferent pigments in the chloroplast absorb different light

The Two Stages of Photosynthesis

Light ReactionDark Reaction
Takes place in the thylakoidTakes place in the stroma
Needs lightDoes not need direct light
Light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH2Carbon dioxide is converted into glucose with the help of ATP and NADPH2 (Calvin cycle)
Water breaks — photolysisGlucose is formed

Photolysis

Photolysis is the breaking of water in light, from which oxygen, protons and electrons come out. The breaking of water in the presence of light is called photolysis.

Why is the Second Stage Called the Dark Reaction?

The second stage of photosynthesis is called the dark reaction because it does not need direct light; it uses the ATP and NADPH2 obtained from the light reaction.

How Carbon Dioxide and Temperature Affect the Rate

  • As carbon dioxide increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases, until other factors run short.
  • As temperature increases, the rate increases.
  • At very high temperature, enzymes are damaged and the rate decreases.

mcqs.q: What is the basic molecule formed during photosynthesis called?
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis, glucose is basically formed. Starch, cellulose and sucrose are substances into which glucose is later converted in plants, but glucose is the basic molecule formed first.

mcqs.q: Where does the light-dependent reaction take place?
mcqs.why: The light reaction takes place in the thylakoid of the chloroplast. The dark reaction, by contrast, takes place in the stroma, so the two stages happen in different parts of the chloroplast.

mcqs.q: What is the breaking of water in the presence of light called?
mcqs.why: The breaking of water in light is called photolysis. From photolysis, oxygen, protons and electrons come out, which is also why photosynthesis produces free oxygen.

mcqs.q: Where does the dark reaction take place, and what is formed in it?
options: In the thylakoid; ATP only is formed
In the stroma; glucose is formed
In the mitochondria; carbon dioxide is formed
In the cytosol; pyruvic acid is formed
mcqs.why: The dark reaction takes place in the stroma and glucose is formed in it. It does not need direct light and uses the ATP and NADPH2 obtained from the light reaction to convert carbon dioxide into glucose.

mcqs.q: What are grana?
options: Stacks of mitochondria in the cell
Drops of stroma in the chloroplast
Stacks of thylakoids in the chloroplast
mcqs.why: Grana are stacks of thylakoids in the chloroplast. They float in the stroma, the semi-fluid protein liquid of the chloroplast, and the thylakoid is where the light reaction takes place.

mcqs.q: What is stroma?
options: The semi-fluid protein liquid of the chloroplast in which grana float
A stack of thylakoids in the chloroplast
A pigment that absorbs different light
The double membrane of the chloroplast
mcqs.why: Stroma is the semi-fluid protein liquid of the chloroplast in which grana float. The dark reaction of photosynthesis takes place in the stroma, where glucose is formed.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis is the only process that ______ free oxygen.
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis is the only process that produces free oxygen. This oxygen comes out when water breaks in light during photolysis, giving oxygen, protons and electrons.

mcqs.q: The reaction in which light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH2 is called the:
mcqs.why: In the light reaction, light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH2. These products are then used in the dark reaction in the stroma to convert carbon dioxide into glucose.

mcqs.q: How does an increase in carbon dioxide affect the rate of photosynthesis?
options: The rate increases, until other factors run short
The rate stops completely at once
There is no effect at all
mcqs.why: As carbon dioxide increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases, until other factors run short. Carbon dioxide is one of the simple inorganic molecules plants use, with water, to form glucose.

mcqs.q: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis at very high temperature, and why?
options: The rate increases because enzymes work faster without limit
The rate decreases because enzymes are damaged
The rate stays exactly the same
The rate decreases because water breaks in light
mcqs.why: As temperature increases the rate of photosynthesis increases, but at very high temperature enzymes are damaged and the rate decreases. This two-part effect of temperature is stated clearly in the source.

lessons.title: 7.3 Respiration
lessons.notes_html:
What is Respiration?

Aerobic respiration is the process in which glucose breaks down in the presence of oxygen and a lot of energy (36 ATP) is obtained. The energy obtained by breaking down a food molecule is stored in the form of ATP.

Breathing and Cellular Respiration

BreathingCellular Respiration
The physical process of air coming in and going outThe chemical process of the breaking down of glucose in the cell, by which energy is obtained

Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

Aerobic RespirationAnaerobic Respiration
Oxygen is usedOxygen is not used
36 ATP are obtainedOnly 2 ATP are obtained
Glucose breaks down in the presence of oxygenGlucose breaks down without oxygen — fermentation, with a little energy obtained

Stages of Aerobic Respiration

StagePlaceWhat Happens
(1) GlycolysisCytosolGlucose breaks into pyruvic acid; a net of 2 ATP are formed
(2) Krebs cycleMitochondriaPyruvic acid breaks down and carbon dioxide comes out
(3) Electron transport chainCristae of mitochondriaATP are formed on the cristae

Total from aerobic respiration: 36 ATP from one mole of glucose.

Pyruvic Acid

Pyruvic acid is the substance formed at the end of glycolysis which goes into the Krebs cycle.

Energy Calculations

  • One mole of glucose gives 2827 kJ of energy — this is the maximum energy obtained from one mole of glucose.
  • For 14135 kJ of energy in the aerobic way: 14135 ÷ 2827 = 5 moles of glucose are used.
  • One mole of glucose gives 36 ATP, so for 180 ATP: 180 ÷ 36 = 5 moles of glucose are used.

Fermentation

Fermentation is the process in which glucose breaks down without oxygen and a little energy is obtained.

Harm of lactic acid fermentation: In lactic acid fermentation, lactic acid collects, which causes tiredness and pain in the muscles.

Respiration and Photosynthesis — Difference

RespirationPhotosynthesis
Glucose breaks down and energy is releasedGlucose is made with light energy
Oxygen is used and carbon dioxide comes outThe reverse happens — carbon dioxide is used and oxygen comes out

mcqs.q: How many ATP are obtained from one mole of glucose in aerobic respiration?
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration is the process in which glucose breaks down in the presence of oxygen and a lot of energy, 36 ATP, is obtained from one mole of glucose. Only 2 ATP are obtained in anaerobic respiration.

mcqs.q: During glycolysis, a small amount of energy is released, enough to produce a net of:
mcqs.why: In glycolysis a net of 2 ATP are formed. Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol, where glucose breaks into pyruvic acid, and only this small amount of energy is released at this stage.

mcqs.q: What is the stage of aerobic respiration that takes place on the cristae of mitochondria called?
mcqs.why: The electron transport chain takes place on the cristae of mitochondria, and ATP are formed there. Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol and the Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondria, but not on the cristae.

mcqs.q: What is the maximum energy obtained from one mole of glucose?
mcqs.why: One mole of glucose gives 2827 kJ of energy, which is the maximum energy obtained from one mole of glucose. This figure is also used to calculate how many moles are needed for a given amount of energy.

mcqs.q: In the aerobic way, 14135 kJ of energy is released. How many moles of glucose are used for this?
mcqs.why: One mole of glucose gives 2827 kJ of energy, so for 14135 kJ, 14135 divided by 2827 equals 5 moles of glucose. Therefore 5 moles of glucose are used to release 14135 kJ in the aerobic way.

mcqs.q: In cellular respiration 180 ATP molecules are formed. How many moles of glucose are used during this process?
mcqs.why: One mole of glucose gives 36 ATP, so for 180 ATP, 180 divided by 36 equals 5 moles of glucose. Therefore 5 moles of glucose are used when 180 ATP molecules are formed.

mcqs.q: What is fermentation?
options: The process in which glucose breaks down without oxygen and a little energy is obtained
The process in which glucose is made with light energy
The physical process of air coming in and going out
The stage that takes place on the cristae of mitochondria
mcqs.why: Fermentation is the process in which glucose breaks down without oxygen and a little energy is obtained. It is the anaerobic way of breaking down glucose, unlike aerobic respiration which uses oxygen and gives 36 ATP.

mcqs.q: What is the harm of lactic acid fermentation?
options: Carbon dioxide collects and damages enzymes
Lactic acid collects, which causes tiredness and pain in the muscles
mcqs.why: In lactic acid fermentation, lactic acid collects, which causes tiredness and pain in the muscles. This collection of lactic acid is the harm of this type of fermentation stated in the source.

mcqs.q: What is pyruvic acid?
options: A pigment in the chloroplast that absorbs light
The substance formed at the end of glycolysis which goes into the Krebs cycle
The semi-fluid protein liquid of the chloroplast
mcqs.why: Pyruvic acid is the substance formed at the end of glycolysis which goes into the Krebs cycle. In glycolysis, glucose breaks into pyruvic acid in the cytosol, and then pyruvic acid breaks down in the mitochondria.

mcqs.q: In the Krebs cycle, what happens and where?
options: Water breaks in light in the thylakoid
Glucose is formed in the stroma
Pyruvic acid breaks down in the mitochondria and carbon dioxide comes out
Air comes in and goes out of the body
mcqs.why: In the Krebs cycle, which takes place in the mitochondria, pyruvic acid breaks down and carbon dioxide comes out. This is the second stage of aerobic respiration, after glycolysis and before the electron transport chain.

mcqs.q: How are breathing and cellular respiration different from each other?
options: Breathing is the physical process of air coming in and going out; cellular respiration is the chemical process of breaking down glucose in the cell
Both are the same physical process
Breathing breaks down glucose in the cell; cellular respiration moves air
Neither of them gives any energy
mcqs.why: Breathing is the physical process of air coming in and going out, while cellular respiration is the chemical process of the breaking down of glucose in the cell, by which energy is obtained. The two must not be confused with each other.

mcqs.q: How many ATP are obtained in anaerobic respiration?
mcqs.why: In anaerobic respiration oxygen is not used and only 2 ATP are obtained. This is much less than aerobic respiration, in which oxygen is used and 36 ATP are obtained from one mole of glucose.

mcqs.q: What is the basic difference between respiration and photosynthesis?
options: There is no difference between them
In respiration glucose breaks down and energy is released; in photosynthesis glucose is made with light energy
In respiration glucose is made; in photosynthesis glucose breaks down
Both processes use oxygen and release carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: In respiration glucose breaks down and energy is released, while in photosynthesis glucose is made with light energy. In respiration oxygen is used and carbon dioxide comes out; in photosynthesis the reverse happens.

mcqs.q: What is aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose breaking down without oxygen, giving only 2 ATP
The breaking of water in light
Glucose breaking down in the presence of oxygen, giving a lot of energy (36 ATP)
The physical process of air coming in and going out
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration is the process in which glucose breaks down in the presence of oxygen and a lot of energy, 36 ATP, is obtained. Its three stages are glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain.

mcqs.q: Where does glycolysis take place, and what is formed at its end?
options: In the cytosol; glucose breaks into pyruvic acid
On the cristae of mitochondria; ATP only
In the stroma; glucose is formed
In the thylakoid; oxygen is formed
mcqs.why: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol, where glucose breaks into pyruvic acid and a net of 2 ATP are obtained. The pyruvic acid formed at the end of glycolysis then goes into the Krebs cycle in the mitochondria.

lessons.title: 8.1 Nutrition in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Nutrition

Nutrition is the way organisms obtain food. Organisms that obtain their food from decayed matter are called saprophytic.

Autotrophic nutritionHeterotrophic nutrition
Organisms make their own food, such as plants.Organisms depend on others for food, such as animals.

Mineral Nutrition in Plants

A fertiliser is a substance in which the nutrients necessary for the food of plants are present. Fertilisers are necessary for plants because from them plants get nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients with which plants grow.

  • Nitrogen: needed by plants because it is required for making proteins and chlorophyll.

Micro-nutrients and Macro-nutrients

MicronutrientsMacronutrients
Nutrients needed by the body in small amounts, such as vitamins and minerals.Nutrients needed in large amounts, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

Types of Fertilisers

Inorganic fertilisersOrganic fertilisers
Made in chemical factories and act quickly, but harm the environment.Made from natural materials, such as dung, and improve the soil.

Environmental Hazards of Chemical Fertilisers

Excessive use of fertilisers damages the ecosystem. Excessive use of chemical fertilisers damages the soil, pollutes water, increases algae in lakes (eutrophication) and increases greenhouse gas in the air. That is why chemical fertilisers are dangerous for the environment.

Important Food Components

ComponentKey point
CarbohydratesCarbohydrates that are digested quickly are called simple carbohydrates.
FatEach gram of fat gives the body about 9 calories, which is double that of carbohydrates and proteins, so fat is called a more powerful food. Fat breaks into fatty acids and glycerol, not starch.
ProteinSeafood is a very good source of protein because it is high in protein and often low in fat.
VitaminsOrganic substances needed in small amounts. Vitamin A is involved in the eye's vision pigment and is necessary for the vision pigment (rhodopsin).

Types of Vitamins

Fat-soluble vitaminsWater-soluble vitamins
A, D, E and K — dissolve in fat and are stored in the body.B and C — dissolve in water and are not stored in the body.

An animal that covers a long distance in migration benefits most from storing energy in the form of fat, because fat stores the most energy.

mcqs.q: Organisms that obtain their food from decayed matter are called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is saprophytic. The source states that organisms which obtain food from decayed matter are called saprophytic, unlike autotrophic organisms which make their own food.

mcqs.q: What is the main difference between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition?
options: Autotrophic organisms make their own food, while heterotrophic organisms depend on others for food
Autotrophic nutrition occurs only in animals
mcqs.why: In autotrophic nutrition organisms make their own food, such as plants. In heterotrophic nutrition organisms depend on others for food, such as animals, so the third option is correct.

mcqs.q: A fertiliser is a substance in which which of the following are present?
options: Nutrients necessary for the food of plants
mcqs.why: A fertiliser contains the nutrients necessary for the food of plants. From fertilisers plants get nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients with which they grow.

mcqs.q: Excessive use of fertilisers does what to the ecosystem?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that excessive use of fertilisers damages the ecosystem. It damages the soil, pollutes water and increases algae in lakes, so it is dangerous for the environment.

mcqs.q: Why is nitrogen needed by plants?
options: It is required for making proteins and chlorophyll
Only to make the leaves red
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is needed by plants because it is required for making proteins and chlorophyll. Without these, the plant cannot grow properly or prepare its food.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes inorganic fertilisers?
options: They are made only from dung
They improve the soil slowly and naturally
They are made in chemical factories, act quickly, but harm the environment
mcqs.why: Inorganic fertilisers are made in chemical factories and act quickly, but they harm the environment. Organic fertilisers, by contrast, are made from natural materials and improve the soil.

mcqs.q: The increase of algae in lakes caused by excessive chemical fertilisers is called:
mcqs.why: Excessive chemical fertilisers pollute water and increase algae in lakes, and this increase of algae is called eutrophication. It is one of the environmental hazards of chemical fertilisers.

mcqs.q: Carbohydrates that are digested quickly are called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is simple carbohydrates. The source states directly that carbohydrates which are digested quickly are called simple carbohydrates.

mcqs.q: Each gram of fat gives the body about how many calories?
mcqs.why: Each gram of fat gives the body about 9 calories, which is double that of carbohydrates and proteins. This is why fat is called a more powerful food.

mcqs.q: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
mcqs.why: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K; they dissolve in fat and are stored in the body. Vitamins B and C are water-soluble and are not stored in the body.

mcqs.q: Vitamin A is correctly matched with which use?
options: It is involved in the eye's vision pigment
It makes red blood cells directly
It digests protein in the stomach
mcqs.why: Vitamin A is involved in the eye's vision pigment and is necessary for the vision pigment, rhodopsin. That is the correctly matched pair given in the source.

mcqs.q: Seafood is a very good source of protein because it is often low in:
mcqs.why: Seafood is high in protein and low in fat, so it is a very good source of protein. The missing word in the source statement is fat.

mcqs.q: Which pair is mismatched?
options: Fat breaks into fatty acids and glycerol
Fat gives about 9 calories per gram
mcqs.why: Fat breaking into starch is the mismatched pair. Fat breaks into fatty acids and glycerol, not starch, while the other three statements about fat are correct.

mcqs.q: Macronutrients are nutrients that are:
options: Needed in small amounts, such as vitamins
Needed in large amounts, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats
Not needed by the body at all
mcqs.why: Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Micronutrients, such as vitamins and minerals, are needed only in small amounts.

mcqs.q: An animal that covers a long distance in migration benefits most from storing energy in the form of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is fat, because fat stores the most energy, giving about 9 calories per gram. A migrating animal therefore stores its energy in the form of fat.

lessons.title: 8.2 Balanced Diet in Relation to Age, Sex and Activity
lessons.notes_html:
Balanced Diet

Food that fulfils all the needs of the body is called a balanced diet. The needs of the body change with age: the period of rapid growth and maturity is called puberty.

Vitamins

Vitamins are organic substances needed by the body in small amounts and necessary for health. Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy.

Malnutrition

Malnutrition is food in which the nutrients needed by the body are not obtained in full amount.

Effects of Malnutrition

  • Growth stops in children
  • Kwashiorkor and marasmus occur
  • Immunity decreases
  • Anaemia occurs
  • Heart diseases, constipation and obesity occur

Starvation is the condition in which the body does not get the food it needs and the body becomes weak. Obesity is the condition in which too much fat collects in the body.

Protein-Deficiency Conditions

MarasmusKwashiorkor
Caused by deficiency of energy (calories) and the child becomes very weak.Caused by deficiency of protein and the body swells.

Protein deficiency in nutrition creates imbalance in the body's system, and this disease is kwashiorkor.

Mineral-Deficiency Diseases

  • Iron: deficiency causes anaemia, and iron deficiency is also related to low immunity. Anaemia is the condition in which the amount of red blood cells or haemoglobin in the blood decreases.
  • Iodine: deficiency causes goitre, which is the swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.
  • Calcium: deficiency makes bones weak and teeth bad. Green leafy vegetables, broccoli and walnuts are sources of calcium; red meat is not a good source of calcium.

mcqs.q: Which disease is caused by deficiency of vitamin C?
mcqs.why: Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy. Goitre is caused by deficiency of iodine and anaemia by deficiency of iron, so each deficiency has its own disease.

mcqs.q: Protein deficiency in nutrition causes which disease?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is kwashiorkor. Protein deficiency creates imbalance in the body's system and causes kwashiorkor, in which the body swells.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between marasmus and kwashiorkor?
options: Both are caused by protein deficiency
Marasmus is caused by deficiency of energy and the child becomes very weak, while kwashiorkor is caused by deficiency of protein and the body swells
Marasmus occurs only in old age
mcqs.why: Marasmus is caused by deficiency of energy (calories) and the child becomes very weak. Kwashiorkor is caused by deficiency of protein and the body swells, which separates the two conditions.

mcqs.q: The period of rapid growth and maturity is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is puberty. The source states that the period of rapid growth and maturity is called puberty, which is why food needs change with age.

mcqs.q: What is goitre?
options: A decrease of red blood cells in the blood
The swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck, caused by deficiency of iodine
A wound in the wall of the stomach
Too much fat collecting in the body
mcqs.why: Goitre is the swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck, caused by deficiency of iodine. It is one of the mineral-deficiency diseases described in the source.

mcqs.q: What is anaemia?
options: Too much sugar in the blood
The condition in which the amount of red blood cells or haemoglobin in the blood decreases
mcqs.why: Anaemia is the condition in which the amount of red blood cells or haemoglobin in the blood decreases. It is caused by deficiency of iron, which is also related to low immunity.

mcqs.q: All of the following are sources of calcium EXCEPT:
mcqs.why: Red meat is the exception, because meat is not a good source of calcium. Green leafy vegetables, broccoli and walnuts are all sources of calcium.

mcqs.q: What is malnutrition?
options: Eating too much food at one time
Eating food at the wrong time
Food in which the nutrients needed by the body are not obtained in full amount
mcqs.why: Malnutrition is food in which the nutrients needed by the body are not obtained in full amount. Its effects include stopped growth in children, weaker immunity and anaemia.

mcqs.q: What is obesity?
options: Too much fat collects in the body
The body does not get the food it needs
mcqs.why: Obesity is the condition in which too much fat collects in the body. It is listed among the effects of malnutrition, together with heart diseases and constipation.

mcqs.q: What are vitamins?
options: Inorganic salts needed in large amounts
The main source of energy for the body
Organic substances needed by the body in small amounts and necessary for health
A type of fat stored in the body
mcqs.why: Vitamins are organic substances needed by the body in small amounts and necessary for health. They are micronutrients, not large-amount energy foods like carbohydrates and fats.

lessons.title: 8.3 Human Digestive System
lessons.notes_html:
Digestion

Digestion is the process in which food breaks into small molecules so that the body can absorb it.

Mechanical digestionChemical digestion
Food is broken into small pieces by chewing and peristalsis.Enzymes break food down chemically.

Parts of the Digestive System in Order

  • Mouth: food is chewed into small pieces and mixed with saliva.
  • Pharynx: the place where the trachea and oesophagus both meet.
  • Oesophagus: food moves onwards from the pharynx.
  • Stomach: food turns into chyme; pepsin breaks protein and acid kills germs.
  • Small intestine: pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal juice break food down completely, and it is absorbed through the villi.
  • Intestines: the remaining part of the digestive tract after digestion in the stomach and small intestine.

The rhythmic and sequential movement of muscles that moves food onwards is called peristalsis.

Action in the Mouth

Chewing is necessary for swallowing because food becomes small pieces, mixes with saliva, and swallowing and digestion become easy.

Action of the Stomach

  • Food turns into chyme, the semi-liquid substance of half-digested food in the stomach.
  • Pepsin starts the digestion of protein in the stomach.
  • The acid kills germs.
  • The stomach protects itself from its acidic environment with a thick layer of mucus which covers the wall of the stomach.

Action of the Small Intestine

  • Bile emulsifies fat in the intestine: it divides fat into small drops so that enzymes can act on it.
  • The juices collected from the pancreas contain different enzymes, such as lipase, amylase and trypsin.
  • Pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal juice break food down completely.
  • The digested food is absorbed through the villi.

mcqs.q: Which statement explains pepsin correctly?
options: It emulsifies fat in the intestine
It digests starch in the mouth
It starts the digestion of protein in the stomach
It is produced by the pancreas
mcqs.why: Pepsin starts the digestion of protein in the stomach. It is a stomach enzyme, while bile emulsifies fat and pancreatic enzymes act in the small intestine.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about bile?
options: It emulsifies fat in the intestine
It is an enzyme that digests protein
It is made inside the stomach
mcqs.why: Bile emulsifies fat in the intestine: it divides fat into small drops so that enzymes can act on it. Bile itself does not digest protein or make chyme.

mcqs.q: In the human digestive system, where do the trachea and oesophagus both meet?
mcqs.why: The trachea and oesophagus both meet in the pharynx. The pharynx is the part behind the mouth from where food passes towards the oesophagus.

mcqs.q: The rhythmic and sequential movement of muscles is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is peristalsis. The sequential movement of muscles is called peristalsis, and this movement pushes food onwards through the digestive system.

mcqs.q: The juices collected from the pancreas contain different:
options: Enzymes, such as lipase, amylase and trypsin
mcqs.why: Pancreatic juice contains different enzymes, such as lipase, amylase and trypsin. These enzymes help break food down completely in the small intestine.

mcqs.q: What is chyme?
options: The semi-liquid substance of half-digested food in the stomach
A vitamin needed in small amounts
mcqs.why: Chyme is the semi-liquid substance of half-digested food in the stomach. In the stomach, food turns into chyme before digestion is completed in the small intestine.

mcqs.q: How does the stomach protect itself from its acidic environment?
options: With a thick layer of mucus which covers the wall of the stomach
mcqs.why: The stomach protects itself from its acidic environment with a thick layer of mucus which covers the wall of the stomach, so the acid does not damage the wall itself.

mcqs.q: Why is chewing necessary for swallowing?
options: It changes the colour of food
Food becomes small pieces, mixes with saliva, and swallowing and digestion become easy
It only makes the teeth strong
mcqs.why: Chewing is necessary because food becomes small pieces, mixes with saliva, and swallowing and digestion become easy. Chewing is the first step of mechanical digestion.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between chemical and mechanical digestion?
options: Both are exactly the same process
Mechanical digestion is done only by enzymes
In mechanical digestion food is broken into small pieces by chewing and peristalsis, while in chemical digestion enzymes break food down chemically
Chemical digestion happens only in the mouth
mcqs.why: In mechanical digestion food is broken into small pieces by chewing and peristalsis. In chemical digestion enzymes break food down chemically, so the third option is correct.

mcqs.q: What is digestion?
options: The process in which food breaks into small molecules so that the body can absorb it
The storage of food in the body
The cooking of food before eating
The making of blood in the body
mcqs.why: Digestion is the process in which food breaks into small molecules so that the body can absorb it. Large molecules cannot be absorbed until digestion has broken them down.

lessons.title: 8.4 Disorders of the Gut
lessons.notes_html:
Constipation

Constipation is the condition in which the belly is not cleared and waste comes out with difficulty. Constipation is also listed among the effects of malnutrition, together with heart diseases and obesity.

Ulcer

An ulcer is a wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines.

How the Stomach Normally Protects Its Wall

The stomach protects itself from its acidic environment with a thick layer of mucus which covers the wall of the stomach. The ulcer is the wound that appears in this inner wall of the stomach or intestines.

Note: this lesson is short because the source material for this unit gives only two gut disorders in detail — constipation and ulcer.

mcqs.q: What is an ulcer?
options: A decrease of red blood cells
A swelling of the thyroid gland
Too much fat in the body
A wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines
mcqs.why: An ulcer is a wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines. It is a disorder of the gut, not a blood condition or a gland swelling.

mcqs.q: What is constipation?
options: The belly is not cleared and waste comes out with difficulty
The belly is cleared again and again with watery waste
Food turns into chyme in the stomach
The thyroid gland swells in the neck
mcqs.why: Constipation is the condition in which the belly is not cleared and waste comes out with difficulty. It is also listed among the effects of malnutrition.

mcqs.q: An ulcer can occur in the inner wall of which organs?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the stomach or intestines, because an ulcer is defined as a wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines.

mcqs.q: In constipation, what happens to the waste?
options: It is absorbed through the villi
mcqs.why: In constipation the belly is not cleared and waste comes out with difficulty. This difficulty in clearing the belly is the main sign of constipation.

mcqs.q: Constipation is listed in the source among the effects of which condition?
mcqs.why: The effects of malnutrition include heart diseases, constipation and obesity. So constipation is one of the effects of malnutrition listed in the source.

mcqs.q: How does the stomach protect its own wall from its acid?
options: With a layer of bone over the wall
With a thick layer of mucus which covers the wall of the stomach
mcqs.why: The stomach protects itself from its acidic environment with a thick layer of mucus which covers its wall. An ulcer, by contrast, is a wound in that inner wall.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a disorder of the gut?
mcqs.why: The ulcer is a disorder of the gut because it is a wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines. Goitre, scurvy and anaemia are deficiency conditions, not gut wounds.

mcqs.q: Which statement about constipation is correct?
options: It is a wound in the stomach wall
It is caused by deficiency of iodine
The belly is not cleared in this condition
It is the swelling of the thyroid gland
mcqs.why: The correct statement is that in constipation the belly is not cleared and waste comes out with difficulty. The other options describe an ulcer, iodine deficiency and goitre.

mcqs.q: What is starvation?
options: The condition in which the body does not get the food it needs and the body becomes weak
The condition in which too much fat collects in the body
A wound in the inner wall of the stomach
The period of rapid growth and maturity
mcqs.why: Starvation is the condition in which the body does not get the food it needs and the body becomes weak. It is different from obesity, in which too much fat collects in the body.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches a gut disorder with its meaning?
options: Ulcer — swelling of the thyroid gland
Ulcer — wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines
mcqs.why: The correct pair is ulcer with a wound in the inner wall of the stomach or intestines. Constipation means the belly is not cleared, and the other pairs describe goitre, anaemia and scurvy.

lessons.title: 9.1 Transport in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
The Root: Entry of Water and Minerals

Water and mineral salts enter the plant through the root. The outer layer of the root is the epidermis, and some of its cells grow out to form root hairs. The part of the root between the endodermis and the epidermis is called the cortex.

Root Hairs

Root hairs are very important for the plant because they increase the absorbing surface. By increasing the surface area, root hairs allow the root to absorb more water and minerals from the soil.

  • Root hairs grow out from the epidermis of the root
  • They increase the surface area for absorption
  • More surface area means more water and minerals are absorbed

Osmosis

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from higher concentration to lower concentration. More exactly, osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. Water enters the root hairs and moves through the cortex by this process.

TermMeaning
CortexThe part of the root between the endodermis and the epidermis
Root hairsOutgrowths of the epidermis that increase the absorbing surface area
OsmosisMovement of water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from higher to lower concentration

mcqs.q: Root hairs are very important for the plant because they:
mcqs.why: Root hairs increase the surface area of the root, so more water and minerals can be absorbed from the soil.

mcqs.q: Root hairs increase the ______ for absorption.
mcqs.why: Root hairs increase the surface area of the root, and a larger surface area allows greater absorption of water and minerals.

mcqs.q: The part of the root between the endodermis and the epidermis is called the:
mcqs.why: The region lying between the endodermis on the inside and the epidermis on the outside of the root is called the cortex.

mcqs.q: The movement of water molecules from higher concentration to lower concentration is called:
mcqs.why: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

mcqs.q: Osmosis takes place through which kind of membrane?
mcqs.why: In osmosis, water molecules pass through a semi-permeable membrane, which allows water through but holds back larger dissolved particles.

mcqs.q: Water and minerals enter the plant mainly through the:
mcqs.why: The root is the organ that absorbs water and mineral salts from the soil and passes them into the plant.

mcqs.q: Which structure is an outgrowth of the root epidermis?
mcqs.why: Root hairs are fine outgrowths of the epidermal cells of the root, formed close behind the root tip.

mcqs.q: If a root had no root hairs, the plant would absorb:
mcqs.why: Without root hairs the absorbing surface area would be much smaller, so the root would take up less water and fewer minerals.

mcqs.q: In osmosis, water molecules move from:
options: The leaf to the root only
mcqs.why: Osmosis is defined as the movement of water molecules from higher concentration to lower concentration through a semi-permeable membrane.

mcqs.q: The cortex of the root lies between:
mcqs.why: The cortex is the ground tissue of the root situated between the inner endodermis and the outer epidermis.

lessons.title: 9.2 Transpiration Process
lessons.notes_html:
What is Transpiration?

Transpiration is the loss of water from the inner parts of plants in the form of vapour. This loss of water as vapour is also simply called water loss. Only a small part of the water absorbed by the roots is used by the plant; the rest escapes as vapour, mostly through the leaves.

Stomata and Guard Cells

Stomata are small pores on the surface of leaves through which gases and water vapour pass. The opening and closing of stomata occurs with the help of guard cells, the special cells that surround each stoma.

  • Stomata are small pores on the leaf surface
  • Gases and water vapour pass through stomata
  • Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata

The Dorsiventral Leaf

A dorsiventral leaf is a leaf in which there is a difference between the upper and lower surfaces. Most broad leaves are dorsiventral, and their stomata are mostly on the lower surface.

Mechanism of Transpiration

The mechanism works as a sequence: the stomata open, water evaporates from the leaf cells into the air, and this loss creates a pull in the xylem. This transpiration pull draws more water upward from the roots.

Why Plants Need Transpiration

  • By transpiration, water and minerals rise up through the plant
  • The plant stays cool
  • Food is transported through the plant

Factors Affecting Transpiration

FactorEffect on Transpiration
TemperatureHigher temperature increases the rate of transpiration
HumidityHigher humidity decreases the rate of transpiration
WindWind carries the vapour away and increases the rate
Atmospheric pressureLower atmospheric pressure increases the rate of transpiration

mcqs.q: Loss of water from the inner parts of plants in the form of vapour is called:
mcqs.why: Transpiration is the loss of water from the inner parts of the plant in the form of vapour, mainly through the leaves.

mcqs.q: Stomata are:
options: Small pores on the surface of leaves
mcqs.why: Stomata are small pores on the surface of leaves through which gases and water vapour pass in and out.

mcqs.q: The opening and closing of stomata occurs with the help of:
mcqs.why: Each stoma is surrounded by guard cells, and the opening and closing of the stomata occurs with these guard cells.

mcqs.q: A dorsiventral leaf is a leaf in which:
options: Both surfaces are exactly the same
There are no stomata at all
Water is stored in large amounts
There is a difference between the upper and lower surfaces
mcqs.why: In a dorsiventral leaf the upper and lower surfaces differ from each other in structure and appearance.

mcqs.q: Plants need transpiration because by it:
options: Water and minerals rise up and the plant stays cool
mcqs.why: Plants need transpiration because by it water and minerals rise up, the plant stays cool, and food is transported.

mcqs.q: In the mechanism of transpiration, evaporation of water from the leaf creates:
mcqs.why: When stomata open and water evaporates, a pull is created in the xylem which draws water upward through the plant.

mcqs.q: Which factor decreases the rate of transpiration when it increases?
mcqs.why: When the humidity of the air is high, the air is already full of water vapour, so the rate of transpiration falls.

mcqs.q: Through stomata, which of the following pass?
mcqs.why: Stomata are the small pores through which gases and water vapour pass between the leaf and the outside air.

mcqs.q: Water loss from a plant means:
options: Loss of minerals from the soil
Loss of water in the form of vapour
Loss of food from the leaves
mcqs.why: Water loss is the loss of water from plants in the form of vapour, and this process is called transpiration.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly shows the mechanism of transpiration?
options: Phloem opens, sucrose sinks, stomata close
Stomata open, water evaporates, a pull is created in the xylem
Guard cells divide, blood flows, heart beats
Roots close, leaves fall, food is stored
mcqs.why: The mechanism of transpiration is: stomata open, water evaporates from the leaf, and a pull is created in the xylem that draws water upward.

lessons.title: 9.3 Transport of Water and Food in the Stem
lessons.notes_html:
The Two Transport Tissues

In flowering plants, transport through the stem is carried out by two tissues. Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves. Phloem carries food (sucrose) from the leaves to other parts of the plant. Organic substances (food) are transported through the phloem.

Structure of Xylem

In flowering plants, xylem is made of four types of tissues:

  • Tracheids
  • Vessels
  • Xylem parenchyma
  • Xylem fibres

How Water Moves in the Xylem

Water rises in the xylem by three forces working together: the pull of transpiration of water from the leaf, the sticking of water molecules to each other, and root pressure. The transpiration pull is the main force that draws the water column upward.

Structure of Phloem: The Sieve Plate

A sieve plate is the wall with pores between the tubes of phloem through which food passes. Food solution moves from one sieve tube to the next through these pores.

Source and Sink

Phloem transport of sucrose can be described as a moving mechanism from "source" to "sink". The source is the part where food is made, such as the leaf. A sink is the part of the plant where food is stored or used. The sink can be both a storage organ and a growing part of the plant.

XylemPhloem
Carries water and mineralsCarries food (sucrose)
From roots to leavesFrom leaves (source) to storage or growing parts (sink)
Made of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibresContains sieve tubes joined by sieve plates

mcqs.q: Organic substances (food) are transported in plants through the:
mcqs.why: Organic substances, that is the food made in the leaves, are transported through the phloem to all parts of the plant.

mcqs.q: Water moves up through the xylem mainly by the pull of:
options: Transpiration of water from the leaf
mcqs.why: Water rises in the xylem by the pull created when water transpires from the leaf, together with the sticking of water molecules and root pressure.

mcqs.q: In flowering plants, xylem is made of how many types of tissues?
mcqs.why: In flowering plants the xylem is made of four types of tissues: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a tissue of xylem?
mcqs.why: The sieve tube belongs to the phloem, not the xylem. Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

mcqs.q: A sieve plate is:
options: The wall with pores between the tubes of phloem
A type of white blood cell
A layer of the root cortex
mcqs.why: A sieve plate is the porous wall between the tubes of phloem through which food passes from one tube to the next.

mcqs.q: In phloem transport, the "sink" is:
options: Both the storage organ and the growing part
mcqs.why: The sink is the part where food is stored or used, so it can be both a storage organ and a growing part of the plant.

mcqs.q: A sink is the part of the plant where food is:
mcqs.why: A sink is defined as the part of the plant where food is stored or used, such as a storage organ or a growing part.

mcqs.q: Xylem carries ______ from the roots to the leaves.
mcqs.why: Xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem carries food from the leaves.

mcqs.q: Phloem carries ______ from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
mcqs.why: Phloem carries food in the form of sucrose from the leaves, where it is made, to the other parts of the plant.

mcqs.q: Water rises in the xylem by the pull of transpiration, the sticking of water molecules, and:
mcqs.why: Three forces raise water in the xylem: the transpiration pull, the sticking (cohesion) of water molecules, and root pressure from below.

lessons.title: 9.4 Transport in Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Why Animals Need a Transport System

In multicellular animals, many cells lie far from the body surface, so simple diffusion cannot supply them. Animals therefore have a circulatory system in which blood carries food, oxygen and waste materials to and from the cells of the body.

Open Circulatory System

In an open circulatory system, blood flows in open spaces outside vessels. The blood leaves the vessels and bathes the tissues directly in open spaces before returning to the heart.

Closed Circulatory System

In a closed circulatory system, blood always stays in vessels. The type of circulatory system in which blood flows through vessels is called the closed circulatory system. Man and other mammals have a closed circulatory system.

Open Circulatory SystemClosed Circulatory System
Blood flows in open spaces outside vesselsBlood always stays inside vessels
Blood comes into direct contact with the tissues in open spacesBlood remains within arteries, veins and capillaries

Because the blood stays inside vessels in a closed system, it can be pumped around the body quickly and under pressure, which suits large and active animals.

mcqs.q: The circulatory system in which blood flows through vessels is called:
mcqs.why: When blood flows through vessels and always stays inside them, the system is called a closed circulatory system.

mcqs.q: In an open circulatory system, blood flows:
mcqs.why: In an open circulatory system the blood flows in open spaces outside vessels and bathes the tissues directly.

mcqs.q: In a closed circulatory system, blood:
options: Leaves the vessels into open spaces
mcqs.why: The defining feature of a closed circulatory system is that the blood always stays within the vessels.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about the open circulatory system?
options: Blood pressure in it is very high
Blood flows in open spaces outside vessels
mcqs.why: In the open type, blood leaves the vessels and flows through open spaces around the tissues before returning.

mcqs.q: Man has which type of circulatory system?
mcqs.why: In man, as in other mammals, the blood always remains inside vessels, so the circulatory system is closed.

mcqs.q: The main difference between open and closed circulatory systems is:
options: Whether blood stays in vessels or flows in open spaces
The size of the animal only
mcqs.why: The two systems differ in the path of blood: in the open system blood flows in open spaces outside vessels, while in the closed system it always stays in vessels.

mcqs.q: Blood in a closed circulatory system is carried by:
mcqs.why: In a closed system the blood circulates through a network of vessels: arteries, veins and capillaries.

mcqs.q: Which of the following describes blood flow in vessels only?
mcqs.why: A closed circulatory system is the type in which blood flows only through vessels and never into open body spaces.

mcqs.q: In an open circulatory system, the tissues are bathed by blood in:
mcqs.why: Because there are no vessels around the tissues in an open system, blood collects in open spaces and bathes the tissues there.

mcqs.q: A closed circulatory system is more suitable for large active animals because blood:
options: Can be pumped quickly under pressure inside vessels
Is not needed by the cells
mcqs.why: With blood enclosed in vessels, the heart can pump it rapidly and under pressure to all cells, which large active animals require.

lessons.title: 9.5 Transport in Man
lessons.notes_html:
Blood: The Transport Fluid

Blood is a red fluid which transports food, oxygen and waste in the body. It has two main parts: plasma (55%), which contains water, proteins and nutrients; and corpuscles, the blood cells.

Composition of Blood

ComponentFunction / Feature
Plasma (55%)The fluid part; contains water, proteins and nutrients
Red blood cells (RBC)Carry oxygen; have no nucleus
White blood cells (WBC)Protect against diseases; have a nucleus
PlateletsClot the blood

Plasma Proteins and Granulocytes

Human plasma proteins include fibrinogen and albumin. Haemoglobin is not a plasma protein; it is found inside the red blood cells. Granulocytes are a type of white blood cells which contain granules. The type of cancer affecting the bone marrow is called leukaemia.

Structure of the Heart

The heart is the pumping organ of the circulatory system and is protected in the pericardium. It is divided into four chambers, and blood flows through them in a fixed sequence: deoxygenated blood returning to the heart first flows into the right atrium, then passes to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs; oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, then passes to the left ventricle, which pumps it to the whole body. The heart has tricuspid, bicuspid and semilunar valves. Semilunar valves are valves that let blood flow in one direction only and stop it from flowing back.

  • Right atrium — receives deoxygenated blood from the body
  • Right ventricle — pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs
  • Left atrium — receives oxygenated blood from the lungs
  • Left ventricle — pumps oxygenated blood to the body

The Two Circuits

In the pulmonary circuit, blood goes from the heart to the lungs and from the lungs back to the heart. In the systemic circuit, blood goes from the heart to all the organs of the body and back to the heart.

Heartbeat and Blood Pressure

The rhythmic pumping of blood by the heart throughout the body is called the heartbeat (pulse). Blood pressure is the pressure which blood exerts on the walls of the vessels.

Blood Vessels

ArteriesVeinsCapillaries
Carry blood from the heart to the organs; walls are thickCarry blood from the organs to the heart; walls are thinMade of a single layer of endothelium so substances can easily pass through them

Atherosclerosis

In atherosclerosis, fat collects in the vessels and the flow of blood stops. A blockage in the brain causes a stroke, and a blockage in the heart causes a heart attack.

mcqs.q: Blood is a red fluid which transports:
options: Food, oxygen and waste in the body
mcqs.why: Blood is the red transport fluid of the body; it carries food, oxygen and waste materials to and from the cells.

mcqs.q: Plasma makes up about what percentage of blood?
mcqs.why: Blood has two main parts: plasma, which forms about 55% of the blood, and the corpuscles, which form the rest.

mcqs.q: Human plasma proteins include:
mcqs.why: Plasma proteins include fibrinogen and albumin. Haemoglobin is not in plasma; it is present inside the red blood cells.

mcqs.q: Deoxygenated blood returning to the human heart first flows into the:
mcqs.why: Deoxygenated blood returning from the body first enters the right atrium of the heart.

mcqs.q: The type of cancer affecting the bone marrow is called:
mcqs.why: Leukaemia is the type of cancer that affects the bone marrow, where blood cells are produced.

mcqs.q: The rhythmic pumping of blood by the heart throughout the body is called:
mcqs.why: The rhythmic pumping action of the heart that sends blood throughout the body is called the heartbeat, felt as the pulse.

mcqs.q: Granulocytes are:
options: Red blood cells without a nucleus
A type of white blood cells which contain granules
mcqs.why: Granulocytes are white blood cells that contain granules in their cytoplasm; they help protect the body against disease.

mcqs.q: Blood pressure is:
options: The amount of plasma in blood
The pressure blood exerts on the walls of the vessels
The number of heartbeats per minute
The pressure of air in the lungs
mcqs.why: Blood pressure is defined as the pressure which the blood exerts on the walls of the blood vessels as it flows through them.

mcqs.q: In the pulmonary circuit, blood goes:
options: From the heart to all organs and back
From the heart to the lungs and from the lungs to the heart
From the lungs to the stomach only
From the body into the right ventricle only
mcqs.why: In the pulmonary circuit blood travels from the heart to the lungs, picks up oxygen there, and returns from the lungs to the heart.

mcqs.q: In the systemic circuit, blood goes:
options: From the roots to the leaves
Only between the heart and the lungs
Only through capillaries of the skin
From the heart to all the organs of the body and back to the heart
mcqs.why: In the systemic circuit blood is pumped from the heart to all the organs of the body and then returns back to the heart.

mcqs.q: Arteries differ from veins because arteries:
options: Carry blood from the heart to the organs and have thick walls
Have a single layer of endothelium
Carry blood from organs to the heart and have thin walls
mcqs.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the organs and have thick walls, while veins carry blood from the organs to the heart and have thin walls.

mcqs.q: Red blood cells differ from white blood cells because RBC:
options: Have a nucleus and fight disease
Carry oxygen and have no nucleus
mcqs.why: Red blood cells carry oxygen and have no nucleus, whereas white blood cells protect against diseases and possess a nucleus.

mcqs.q: Capillaries are made of a single layer of endothelium so that:
options: Blood flows back to the heart
Substances can easily pass through them
mcqs.why: The single thin layer of endothelium in capillaries allows substances to pass easily between the blood and the tissues.

mcqs.q: Semilunar valves are valves that:
options: Let blood flow in one direction only and stop it flowing back
mcqs.why: Semilunar valves allow blood to flow in one direction only and prevent it from flowing back into the heart chambers.

mcqs.q: In atherosclerosis, a blockage in the brain causes ______ and a blockage in the heart causes ______.
mcqs.why: In atherosclerosis fat collects in the vessels and blocks blood flow: a blockage in the brain causes a stroke, and a blockage in the heart causes a heart attack.
